title: Revelation 3:7–13
context: To Philadelphia Christ presents himself as the holy and true one who holds the key of David and opens doors no one can shut. The church has little power but has kept his word and not denied his name. He promises to vindicate it before its opponents, to keep it from the coming hour of testing, and to make the overcomer a permanent pillar in God’s temple, marked with God’s name.

verses.text: “To the angel of the assembly in Philadelphia write: “He who is holy, he who is true, he who has the key of David, he who opens and no one can shut, and who shuts and no one opens, says these things:
verses.arminianNotes: The key of David echoes Isaiah 22:22, where authority over the king’s house is given to Eliakim. Christ holds that authority now, and what he opens no one can shut. Arminian readers take this as the sovereign authority of the risen Lord over access to the kingdom, exercised in a way that still calls for faithful response from the church.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear a strong statement of Christ’s sovereignty: he opens and no one can shut, and he shuts and no one opens. Access to God’s house rests in his hands. Many Reformed interpreters connect this with Christ’s power to open hearts and doors for the gospel, which no human opposition can undo.

verses.text: “I know your works (behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one can shut), that you have a little power, and kept my word, and didn’t deny my name.
verses.arminianNotes: The open door is most often read as an opportunity for mission or as entry into the kingdom. Philadelphia has little power, yet it has kept Christ’s word and not denied his name. Arminian readers see faithfulness under pressure that Christ commends, and an opportunity he sets before a weak church to use.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the door is set before the church by Christ, and no one can shut it. The church’s weakness highlights that its standing and fruitfulness come from him. Its faithfulness in keeping his word is commended as the fruit of his keeping power.

verses.text: Behold, I make some of the synagogue of Satan, of those who say they are Jews, and they are not, but lie—behold, I will make them to come and worship before your feet, and to know that I have loved you.
verses.arminianNotes: The “synagogue of Satan” refers to local opponents who claimed the name of God’s people while rejecting Christ. The promise is vindication: these opponents will come to know that Christ has loved this church. Arminian readers often stress that this does not license hostility toward Jewish people, and that the language concerns a specific local conflict.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the verse as a reversal of Isaiah 60:14, where the nations bow before Israel. The true people of God are now those who belong to Christ, Jew and Gentile together. The promise that the opponents will know “I have loved you” is a comfort grounded in Christ’s electing love for his church. The language reflects a local conflict and is not a warrant for contempt toward Jewish people.

verses.text: Because you kept my command to endure, I also will keep you from the hour of testing which is to come on the whole world, to test those who dwell on the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: “I also will keep you from the hour of testing” is read in different ways. Some take it as protection through the trial, and others take it as removal from it. Pretribulational futurists see a promise of the church’s removal before a coming tribulation, while many others read it as preservation of faith during worldwide trouble. Arminian readers note that the promise is linked to the church’s having kept Christ’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers commonly read the promise as preservation in the trial, comparing John 17:15, where Jesus prays not that the Father take the disciples out of the world but that he keep them from the evil one. Historicist, preterist, and idealist readings differ on what the hour of testing refers to, but most Reformed interpreters agree that Christ keeps his people faithful through it.

verses.text: I am coming quickly! Hold firmly that which you have, so that no one takes your crown.
verses.arminianNotes: “Hold firmly that which you have, so that no one takes your crown” is a call to persevere. Arminian readers take it as a warning that the crown can be lost if the church lets go of what it has received. The nearness of Christ’s coming adds urgency.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the same command as one of the means by which Christ preserves his people. The crown is the reward of victory, and believers are urged to hold fast. The warning keeps them watchful, while the promise of verse 10 assures them that Christ himself is keeping them.
verses.keyContrast: Arminian readers take “so that no one takes your crown” as a sign that perseverance is not guaranteed and that the crown can be lost. Reformed readers see the warning as a means Christ uses to keep his people, who will persevere because he is keeping them.

verses.text: He who overcomes, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he will go out from there no more. I will write on him the name of my God and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down out of heaven from my God, and my own new name.
verses.arminianNotes: The overcomer becomes a pillar in God’s temple and will go out from there no more. For a city often shaken by earthquakes, the image is one of stability. Arminian readers take the permanence as the final state of those who have overcome, after the time of testing is over.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see here the security of God’s people, marked with the name of God, the city, and Christ. Being named belongs to God’s ownership. The promise that they will go out no more is a picture of the permanence of salvation.

verses.text: He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the assemblies.
verses.arminianNotes: The refrain again extends the message to all the churches. Arminian readers stress that each hearer must respond to the Spirit’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Spirit’s word reaches every church, and those whom he enables will hear it and hold fast.
